title: The Supreme Court First Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Shrunk Them: From Flag Salutes to Backpack Searches
dek: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six rulings trace the arc of public school students' constitutional rights; the Court, having declared that schools are not 'enclaves of totalitarianism,' also upheld corporal punishment and searches based on reasonable suspicion, narrowing those rights.
why: Each case is explained in five or six minutes, covering background and key holdings—ideal for listeners who want a single overview of the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment, and searches in American public schools.
who: Parents, middle and high school teachers, and law students, as well as anyone seeking to understand the limits of government power and children's rights in American public schools.
skip: Listeners familiar with the Establishment Clause can skip the second case; if you know the earlier cases well, jump to the corporal punishment and search cases after 25:40.

points.h: The Flag-Salute Case: Students' Rights Enter the Schoolhouse
points.body: Can students really assert First Amendment rights during the school day? The case actually began with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families believed saluting the flag violated the commandments against other gods and graven images, so they refused. In 1940 the Supreme Court ruled against them, and World War II led more districts to require daily salutes and pledges. West Virginia expelled students who refused and listed them as delinquents; parents could be fined or jailed. In 1943, the Court reversed 6–3. Justice Jackson wrote on Flag Day: no official can prescribe orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or other matters; students need not confess beliefs they do not hold or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court recognized that students have some First Amendment rights at school.

During the Cold War, America cast itself as a God-fearing nation, adding 'Under God' to the Pledge in 1954, and more public schools began daily Bible reading or prayer. In 1951, New York's Board of Regents asked religious leaders to compose a short, nondenominational prayer; districts could choose whether to adopt it. The district that used it allowed students to opt out, but parents of ten students sued anyway. In 1962, Engel v. Vitale struck it down 6–1. The key was not coercion but that the prayer was written by government, which itself established religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: the first experiment with our liberties should raise the alarm; the same power that can establish Christianity to the exclusion of all other religions can also establish one sect of Christianity. The decision sparked backlash, and the plaintiff families faced ridicule and harassment.

In December 1965, Des Moines middle and high school students planned to wear black armbands to protest U.S. involvement in Vietnam. The school announced that refusing to remove them would lead to suspension; some students—including four siblings—wore them and were suspended. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7–2. The issue was not ordinary dress codes but a quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Without evidence of actual or reasonably foreseeable material disruption, schools could not suppress student opinion. The opinion declared that public schools are not 'enclaves of totalitarianism' and that students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This 'substantial disruption' standard became the benchmark for campus speech. Justice Black dissented, predicting students would defy nearly all rules; the hosts note that this slippery-slope argument sounds quite absurd.

In 1983, Hazelwood East High School's student newspaper, The Spectrum, had two articles that troubled Principal Reynolds: one on teen pregnancy used pseudonyms but might still identify the interviewee, and a divorce story named a student's parent critically. Reynolds decided to delete the entire two pages rather than just the articles, citing lack of time to edit and the need to publish before semester's end. In 1988, the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5–3. The key distinction was between 'tolerating student speech' and 'promoting student speech': the paper was funded by the school, readers would see it as bearing the school's imprimatur, and the articles were indeed immature journalistically. The Court held that schools may regulate what they sponsor. This drew the first clear boundary around Tinker's rights.

points.h: Corporal Punishment Is Not Cruel and Unusual
points.body: Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many teachers once kept wooden paddles on their desks, and research showed corporal punishment has not disappeared in America. In 1977's Ingram v. Wright, the school's board was less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, and half an inch thick, with a usual range of one to five blows; but Ingram received more than 20 blows in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Court did not decide whether that particular punishment was excessive; it ruled that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The Eighth Amendment protects convicted persons; prisoners and schoolchildren are separated by the 'harsh facts of criminal conviction and incarceration.' Schools are open places with teachers and peers as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA statistics, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually used in 14; boys, Black students, and students with disabilities are struck at significantly higher rates.

points.h: Searching a Purse Needs Only Reasonable Suspicion
points.body: In 1980, a 14-year-old New Jersey student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice Principal Choplik searched her purse, found cigarettes and rolling papers, then continued and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing. TLO was convicted and given one year of probation. In 1985, the Supreme Court upheld the search 6–3. The Court acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment applies to school officials and that students have an expectation of privacy, but it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. Therefore, school searches need not meet the probable cause standard required for police; a lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and the purse was the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was also reasonable.

terms.def: The standard from Tinker for disciplining student speech: schools need actual or reasonably foreseeable material disruption of school activities.
The First Amendment provision barring government establishment or endorsement of religion; originally applied only to the federal government, later extended to states via the Fourteenth Amendment.
A lower evidentiary threshold than probable cause, applied to school officials' searches of students and their belongings.
The higher standard required for police arrests or searches; contrasted here with the reasonable suspicion standard for in-school searches.
Punishment that inflicts physical pain; in this episode, specifically paddling students on the buttocks with a wooden board.

Students in school as well as out of school are persons under our Constitution.
